questions.question: In a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$, what does it mean for $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ to be a boundary point of $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \boldsymbol{X}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ must lie inside $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{x}_0$ must lie outside $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is the centre of a ball contained in $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is neither interior nor exterior to $\boldsymbol{E}$.
questions.explanation: A boundary point of $E$ is one that is neither an interior point nor an exterior point of $E$. Equivalently, every ball around it meets both $E$ and its complement.
questions.source_support: The definition says a boundary point is neither an interior nor an exterior point.

A boundary point need not lie outside $E$; e.g., $0$ is a boundary point of $[0,1]$ and $0\in[0,1]$.
Having a ball contained in $E$ describes an interior point, not a boundary point.
